author: Greg Abel
title: Berkshire Hathaway 2025 Shareholder Letter
headline: Abel’s first letter as CEO: the culture stays, more than $370 billion waits for the right pitch, and Kraft Heinz is called a disappointment.
summary: Greg Abel’s first annual letter writes Berkshire’s values down and promises they will not change. Operating earnings fell to $44.5 billion from $47.4 billion. Insurance had an exceptional underwriting year (87.1% combined ratio), but Abel expects to write less business as prices soften. Cash and Treasuries above $370 billion are dry powder, he says, not a retreat. 2025 brought two acquisitions, OxyChem and Bell Laboratories. The core stocks (Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola, Moody’s and the five Japanese trading houses) stay, with little activity planned.

takeaways.label: Move
takeaways.text: Bought two businesses in 2025: OxyChem, which Berkshire got to know through its Occidental stake, and the rodent-control maker Bell Laboratories.

takeaways.label: View
takeaways.text: Cash and Treasuries above $370 billion are dry powder. Buybacks only happen below a conservative estimate of intrinsic value.

takeaways.label: View
takeaways.text: Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola, Moody’s and the Japanese trading houses make up nearly two-thirds of the $297.8 billion stock portfolio. Activity there will be limited.

takeaways.label: Watch
takeaways.text: Insurance prices are softening, so Berkshire expects to write less property-casualty insurance and reinsurance for a while.

takeaways.label: Watch
takeaways.text: BNSF’s 34.5% operating margin still trails the best railroads. Each point of margin is worth about $230 million of cash flow a year.

risks.text: More capital in insurance is cutting property reinsurance prices, while claims inflation outpaces pricing in casualty.
GEICO’s rate increases restored margins but cost customers; competitors’ rate cuts may keep retention under pressure in 2026.
Wildfire liability at the utilities, and AI-driven power demand that BHE will only serve if data-centre customers pay for the grid it needs.

quotes.text: Many times in Berkshire’s history, some observers have suggested that our substantial cash position signals a retreat from investing. It does not.
Our investment in Kraft Heinz has been disappointing.
At Berkshire’s scale, the math of compounding works against us – a reality long understood and best acknowledged plainly.

stocks.note: Largest holding, $62.0 billion at year-end. Core, little activity planned.
Return “well short of adequate”, even counting the original Heinz preferred.
Held under the equity method. Berkshire bought its OxyChem unit.
